en: And for the pacification of defects such as those caused by malevolent planets,
for the complete destruction of the suffering of poverty,
and for the sake of increasing the lifespan of those with short lives.
The performance of the *svastyayana* rite with the three circles is highly praised.

For the sake of pacifying misfortunes such as malevolent spirits, for the purpose of utterly destroying the suffering of poverty, and for the cause of increasing the lifespan of those with short lives, the performance of auspicious rites through the three maṇḍalas is thoroughly taught.
Therefore, for the sake of one's own welfare and for the pacification of the afflictions of the planets and so forth,
this should be performed by those with perfectly pure minds.
It was proclaimed by the Buddhas for the sake of the welfare of the world.

Therefore, with the intention of benefiting oneself, one should pacify the faults of malevolent spirits; for this ritual was taught by the Buddhas, who possess utterly pure minds, as a cause for the welfare of living beings.
Furthermore, the drawing of the lines for the Maṇḍala of the Mothers of the Planets (Grahamātṛkā) is described:
having left a space of four mātrās within the root [line], one should draw the line.
One should draw the lines for the mandala of the Planets and Mothers; furthermore, having excluded four small units from within the root line, [one should proceed].
In this case, it should be given to the mantra-practitioners up to the limit of the two diagonal lines;
furthermore, one should subsequently cause a circle to be made within that as well.
The mantrin should offer there between the two diagonal lines; within that, one should draw a circle reaching to its very edge.
Furthermore, within the interval of the measure, one should draw a row of vajras there;
the remainder should be made into an eight-petaled lotus, and that should be divided into three parts.
Rotate it once more from one small part; there, fashion a vajra garland. As for the remainder, divide it into three parts and fashion an eight-petaled lotus.
There, the knower of mantras should cause the removal of the corner-lines and so forth;
having discarded the line within the base, at a distance equal to the door.
The side-lines and so forth should be distinguished by one skilled in the secret mantra; within the central line, one should leave a space reaching to the doors.
Within that [mandala] as well, there is a thread at a distance of four *mātrās*;
likewise, the remaining eight-petalled lotus is slightly larger in measurement.
Furthermore, one should draw the lines within; likewise, up to four small units [of measurement], the remainder shall be complete as an eight-petaled lotus. There is nothing more nor less than this.
One should cause the mandala of Vasudhārā to be constructed according to the prescribed rite;
at the end of the Vedic measures of Brahmā, one should have a single circle made.
The mandala of the Nor-rgyun-ma [Vasudhārā] should be constructed by those skilled in the rituals; one should draw a single circle extending from the Brahma-line to the end of the Ṛgveda.
Then, having abandoned the half-mora, there is the second, the *vṛtta-sūtra*;
then, having omitted four morae, there is the third, the *cāra-vṛtta*.
Then, having set aside half a minor unit, there is the second circular line. Then, having set aside four minor units, there is the third circle for the spokes.
Having abandoned the third *sārdhamātrā*, the fourth is the *nemīvṛtta*;
then, having omitted two *mātrās*, there is the *kesarasūcaka* metre.

Then, up to the complete exclusion of one minor part (*aṃśuka*), there is the fourth circle, the rim (*nemi*). Then, having set aside two minor parts, there is the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) line.
Having left aside the mere circle of the lotus-petal,
one should then draw three circles outside it with an interval of two mātrās each; furthermore, eight lotuses should be drawn on the exterior in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Having set aside the small units (kalā) of the Vidyā, one should draw a circle outside that [lotus] with two small units; furthermore, an eight-petaled lotus should be drawn in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The wheel of Uṣṇīṣavijayā, which bestows the accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings,
should be fashioned by one who possesses the vajra of wisdom and desires the benefit of all sentient beings.
The wheel of complete victory accomplishes all aims; having regard for the benefit of all sentient beings, this should be performed with the vajra of primordial wisdom.
Therein, first, the ritual procedure for the Mothers of the Planets (grahamātṛkā) is written.
First, the ritual procedure for the Mothers of the Planets shall be written.

In the center of the central petal, upon a white lotus and a maṇḍala of saffron-scented paste, one should thus contemplate the Sun-god: bearing the form of an ascetic, red in color, holding a white lotus with both arms, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. To him, milk-food should be offered, along with incense of *kunduru*. One should worship him with the heart-mantra: *oṃ āḥ megholkāya svāhā*.

In the center, upon a white lotus, one should visualize the deity Sūrya on a maṇḍala of saffron fragrance; he assumes the form of an ascetic, is red in color, holds a white water-lily in his two hands, and is equal in brilliance to ten million suns. To him, one should offer an oblation of milk-rice and incense of *kunduru*. Oṃ āḥ.
One should perform the offering with the heart mantra: *me gha au la kha ya svāhā*.

On the eastern petal, upon a red lotus and a Priyaṅgu-scented maṇḍala, is Soma, assuming the form of a Brahmin, white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair, holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his two hands, and adorned with a *kumuda* flower. His incense is fragrant resin (*śrīvāsa*), and his food is rice with ghee. OṂ CANDRĀMṚTAVIKRAMĀYA ŚĪTĀṂŚAVE AḤ SVĀHĀ.

On the eastern petal, upon a red lotus, is a *maṇḍala* of the fragrance of *priyaṅgu*. Therein is the Moon, assuming the form of a Brahmin, white in color, with his hair bound in a topknot; he holds a rosary in one hand and a water-pot containing a *kumuda* flower in the other. To him, an offering of ghee as food and *sihlaka* incense should be presented:
*oṃ candrāmṛtabhikramāyaśita āṃ śve āḥ svāhā*.

On the southern petal, upon a white lotus and a sandalwood-scented mandala, is Maṅgala in the form of a monk. He is red in color, wears red garments and a crown, holds a spear in his left hand, and displays the gesture of granting boons with his right. Food should be offered to him: black gram rice (*māṣabhakta*) or jaggery-rice (*guḍodana*), along with *guggulu* incense. The mantra is: *oṃ namo raktāṅgarasojjvalakumārāya svāhā*.

On the southern petal, upon a white lotus, on a mandala fragrant with sandalwood, is Śrī, who assumes the form of a bhikṣu. His body is red in color, he wears red garments and a crown, holds a *śakti* in his left hand, and performs the gesture of supreme generosity (*varada-mudrā*) with his right. To him, one should offer food consisting of black lentil porridge or molasses porridge, as well as incense of *guggulu*.
[The mantra is: *namo rakta ādgaradzvala kumārāya svāhā*.

On the western petal, upon a red lotus and a mandala of black aloe-wood incense, is the renowned Budha, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). He is yellow in color with a reddish beard, holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his right and left hands respectively. His food is a dish of black gram, mung beans, and sesame. His incense is *gandharasa*. Homage to the very yellow-colored Prince Budha; Oṃ, to Budha, svāhā!

On a mandala of black *akāru* incense upon a red lotus in the western petal, the one renowned as Śukra (Venus) is depicted with the form of a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārin*), his body yellowish-red in color, holding a rosary and a water-pot in his right and left hands respectively. For this deity, the food offering consists of a mixture of mung beans and broad beans, and the incense is *gandharasa*.

*Rāja-sūtra-buddha-sūpita-varṇāya namaḥ | Oṃ buddhāya svāhā |* On the northern petal, upon a white lotus and a fragrant mandala of *devadāru* wood, is the wandering ascetic Bṛhaspati. He has the luster of molten gold and red hair and beard. He holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). His food is curd-rice or milk. The incense is honey and clarified butter. For the emergence of the red color, [the mantra is]: *Bṛhaspataye oṃ namo bhogāspadāya svāhā*.

In the center of a white lotus on the northern petal, upon a *maṇḍala* of the fragrance of *devadāru*, is a ritual dagger (*kīla*) in the form of a monk, possessing the luster of refined gold, with a red beard, holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). For this, the food offering consists of curd-rice or milk-gruel, along with incense of parched grain and clarified butter.
[The mantra is: *lotita varṇa nirgamāya br̥haspate oṃ namo bhogaspadeya svāhā*.

On the southeastern petal, upon a red lotus and a sandalwood-scented maṇḍala, is Śukra, who observes the Pāśupata vow. He is white in color and wears a crown of matted hair. He holds a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Milk-food should be offered to him, along with camphor incense. Oṃ namaḥ śukrādhipataye asurottamāya śuddhe viraje svāhā.

On my petal is a white *maṇḍala* with the scent of sandalwood, where resides Paśupati, who maintains the ascetic observance (*vrata*), is white in color, wears a crown of matted locks, and holds a rosary and a water-pot. To him, one should offer milk-rice as food and camphor incense. Oṃ namaḥ śakrādhipataye asura-uttama-āya śuddhe viraje svāhā.

On the southwestern petal, upon a white lotus and a mandala of blue sandalwood scent, Saturn (Śanaiścara) is to be known as black, naked, with yellow matted hair, crown, and beard; he holds a rosary and a *khikkhirikā* [gourd]. His food is black gram (*māṣa*) rice and sesame porridge (*kṛsara*). Fragrance, flavor, and incense should be offered. *Oṃ śani nīlābhasukṛṣṇāya kṛṣṇavarṇāya kṛṣṇabhuk svāhā*.

On a white lotus in the petal of the Southwest (Nairṛtya), upon a blue *maṇḍala* scented with sandalwood, one should know that Śaniścara is dressed in black garments; he wears a crown of greyish-white matted locks, has a beard, and holds a rosary and a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*). To him, one should offer food consisting of black lentils and incense of *gandharasa*.

Oṃ śanaiścarāya āpasukṛṣṇāya kṛṣṇavarṇabhuja svāhā! On the western petal, upon a red lotus and a circular mandala of piṇḍatagara fragrance, is Rāhu: a Kāpālika, with the luster of the color of lapis lazuli (rājāvarta), possessing half a body, having the sun as his chariot; his pair of eyes are terrifying, his fangs are formidable, and his forehead is furrowed with a frown; he stands in the midst of five-colored clouds, positioned in the gesture of swallowing the moon and sun with both arms. To him, food consisting of fish and meat, or sesame and rice-porridge (kṛsara), should be offered, as well as bilva incense.
Oṃ, homage to the one with a deformed face, to Rāhu who resembles a bee or collyrium, who is fond of nectar; svāhā!

Upon a red lotus with wind-petals, on a mandala of the scent of *paṇḍitakāri*, is Rāhu, possessing a skull-cup; his body is half-seated upon the chariot of the sun, endowed with two terrifying eyes, baring his fangs, with his brows knitted in a frown upon his forehead, and dwelling amidst clouds of five colors.

He abides in the manner of devouring the sun and moon with his hands. For this [deity], there is food prepared from fish, meat, or sesame, and bilva incense. Oṃ namo vikṛtapakvadhīrarāho bhidgānyatsannābhāya āmrita-priyāya svāhā.

On the northeastern petal, upon a red lotus and a mandala of *spṛkkā* fragrance, is Caṇḍālarūpaketu, smoke-colored, with palms joined in reverence. He has the form of a serpent and carries a tail. An offering of food filled with ghee should be given to him, as well as incense made from resinous sap. *Oṃ namaḥ dhūmrābhravarṇasaṃnibhāya jyotiḥketave svāhā*.

On the western petal, upon a red lotus, one should prepare a mandala with the fragrance of blended incense. Therein is Caṇḍa, having the form of a serpent with a long tail, the color of foam, with palms joined and his coiled tail in the manner of a nāga. To him, one should offer oily foods and white incense as an offering.

oṃ namo dhūmrārciṣe jvālina sannibhāya jyotikaṭabhe svāhā | At the eastern gate of the maṇḍala is the Buddha, the Blessed One, golden in color, performing the mudrā of meditative concentration (samādhi).
In the south is Vajrapāṇi, dark green in color;
with his right hand he holds a vajra at his heart, and his left hand rests upon the earth.
At the western gate is red Lokeśvara; his right hand is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) and his left hand performs the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
At the northern gate is red Lokeśvara; his right hand is in the boon-granting gesture and his left hand performs the gesture of fearlessness.
At the northern gate is Mañjuśrīkumāra, saffron-colored, holding the mudrā of turning the wheel of Dharma.
At the northern gate is Mañjuśrīkumāra, saffron-colored, performing the mudrā of teaching the Dharma.
In the northeast are all the planets; they are of various colors, various shapes, and diverse forms.

In the fire [mandala] are all the lunar mansions, each seated upon its own vehicle, all with their palms joined in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture. All the lunar mansions are seated correctly upon their respective vehicles, and all have their palms joined together.
In the southwest (nairṛta) are all calamities; they are of fierce form.
In the direction of the Lord of the Dead (nairṛta), there are all those who cause harm, possessing terrifying forms.

In the northwest is Bhaṭṭārikā Mahāvidyā, with three faces—white, blue, and red. With her two primary hands she displays the gesture of teaching (*vyākhyānamudrā*). In her right [hands] she holds a lotus and a radiating jewel; in her left, she holds a noose and a spear. She wears a jeweled crown, sits in the vajra-posture, rests upon a moon seat, is sixteen years of age, and is adorned with all ornaments.

In the west is Vajravārāhī, the Great Wisdom, with three faces—white, blue, and red. Her primary hands hold the mudrās as previously explained; her right hands hold a lotus and a blazing jewel, and her left hands hold a noose and a śakti.
Wearing a precious crown, seated upon a moon disc in the vajra posture, he is eight years of age and adorned with all ornaments.

Outside the eastern gate of the maṇḍala is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; in the south, Virūḍhaka; in the west, Virūpākṣa; and in the north, Kuvera. They are yellow, black, red, and yellow respectively, and are each equipped with their own respective weapons.

Outside the gates of the maṇḍala, in the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, in the south Virūḍhaka, in the west Virūpākṣa, and in the north Vaiśravaṇa (Kuvera); they are yellow, black, red, and yellow, and are endowed with their own respective hand-symbols.

In that regard, these are the food offerings for the Buddha and the others: milk for the Buddha; milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for Vajrapāṇi; rice with jaggery (*guḍānna*) for Lokeśvara; curd-rice (*dadhyanna*) for Mañjuśrī; rice with ghee for all the planetary deities (*graha*); curd-rice for all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); black-gram rice (*māṣabhakta*) for all calamities; and for the Blessed Lady, milk and fragrant incense.

Regarding the food offerings for the Buddha and the others: for the Buddha, it is rice gruel; for Vajrapāṇi, milk; for Lokeśvara, molasses-rice; for Mañjuśrī, curd-rice; for all the planets (graha), ghee-rice; for all the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), curd-rice; for all the attendants (upacāraka), black lentil-rice; and for the Bhagavatī, milk along with fragrant incense.
For all [the deities], one should offer incense of white sandalwood, banners of their respective colors, ghee-lamps with wicks of their respective colors, and fine cloths of their respective colors.

For all, one should offer the incense of white sandalwood, banners of their respective colors, ghee-lights upon wicks of their respective colors, and also excellent fabrics of their respective colors.

The mantra-words of the Buddha and others: Oṃ namo buddhāya svāhā | Oṃ vajradharāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ padmadharāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ kumārāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ sarvagrahāṇāṃ svāhā | Oṃ sarvanakṣatrāṇāṃ svāhā | Oṃ sarvopadravāṇāṃ svāhā | Oṃ mahāvidye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ dhṛtarāṣṭrāya svāhā | Oṃ virūḍhakāya svāhā | Oṃ virūpākṣāya svāhā | Oṃ kuverāya svāhā ||

The mantra words for the Buddha and others are as follows: Oṃ namo buddhāya svāhā | Oṃ vajradharāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ padmadharāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ kumārāya namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ sarvagrahāṇāṃ namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ sarvanakṣatrāṇāṃ svāhā | Oṃ sarvotpātavānāṃ svāhā ||

oṃ mahāvidye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ dhretaraṣṭāya svāhā | oṃ virūḍhakāya svāhā | oṃ virūpākṣāya svāhā | oṃ kubेराय svāhā | One should offer the *argha* to all of them with their respective mantras as follows.
For all of these, one should offer the water for the feet using their respective mantras themselves.

In that regard, for the Sun, [the offering is made] with red sesame, copper, and red sandalwood; for the Moon, with silver, white sesame, and white sandalwood; for Mars, with copper, red rice, and red sandalwood; for Mercury, with barley, coral, and *khalika*; for Jupiter, with gold, mustard seeds, and *khalika*; for Venus, with pearls, unbroken grains of rice, and white sandalwood; for Saturn, with iron, black beans, and *kastūrī*; for Rāhu, with iron, black sesame, and all types of fragrant substances; and for Ketu, with iron, *muṅga* beans, and fragrant substances.
For the remaining [deities], one should fill a conch with ghee and honey, cast in five jewels, and offer the *argha* oblation.

Furthermore, for the Sun, one should use red sesame, copper, and red sandalwood; for the Moon, silver, white sesame, and white sandalwood; for Maṅgala (Mars), copper, red rice, and red sandalwood; for Budha (Mercury), barley, coral, and saffron; and for Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), gold, white mustard seeds, and saffron.

For Paṅsaṅla, [one should offer] pearls, parched rice, and white sandalwood; for Spenpa, iron, black lentils, and *gla rtsi*; for Sgra gcan, iron, black sesame seeds, and all types of perfumes; for Mjug ring, iron, *mudga* beans, and excellent fragrances.
For the remaining [vessels], fill them with honey and ghee, place the five precious gems inside, and offer them as an oblation of water (argham).

Having contemplated that [the deity] has become of one flavor through the procedure of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing with the mantras *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, and having worshipped with the previously mentioned flowers, incense, and so forth using their respective mantras, one should perform the worship for all of them there in due order and recite the heart-mantras of the nine planets one hundred and eight times each.

Having visualized that [the deity] has become of equal taste through the ritual of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing with the mantra *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, one should worship perfectly with the individual mantras using the previously explained flowers, incense, and so forth.
Then, having performed all these offerings in their proper sequence, one should recite each of the mantras of all the planets one hundred and eight times.
Thereafter,
one should recite seven times the dhāraṇī called the Mother of the Planets (Grahamātṛkā).

Then, having recited the heart-mantra of Grahāmātṛkā one hundred and eight times, or a thousand times, or as many times as one is able, and having prayed for the accomplishment of one's desired goal, one should stabilize it with the hundred-syllable mantra, dismiss [the deity] according to the ritual rules, and cause [the image] to be carried away in the waters of a river or similar body of water as previously described.

Then, having recited the essence mantra of the Mother of the Planets one hundred and eight times, or one thousand times, or as much as possible, one should request the desired siddhi, stabilize it with the hundred-syllable mantra, request the deity to depart according to the ritual procedure, and cast [the materials] into the waters of a river as before.
Thereafter, one should feed the preceptor and others with food free from meat, and should give gifts and so forth according to one's ability.
Thereafter, the master and others should partake of blameless food and offer gifts and so forth according to their ability.
This is the ritual for the *grahamātṛkā-svastyanaya* (the auspicious rite of the Mothers of the Planets). || O ||
Thus concludes the ritual for bringing about well-being through the planetary consorts.
I shall explain the ritual procedure for Vasudhārā.
The ritual of Vasudhārā shall now be explained.

Immediately following the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), upon a yellow lotus transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ*, there is a moon disc formed from the syllable *a*. Above that, there is a mountain of jewels transformed from the syllable *vuṃ*, and upon that as well, one should visualize Vasudhārā from the seed-syllable *vlūṃ*. She is yellow in color, with one face and six arms, seated in the *lalita* posture, and wearing a crown of Tathāgatas. With her first right hand she displays the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*) while revealing a treasure; with the second, she rains down jewels.

With the third [hand], she performs a salutation to the Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa. One should meditate on her as possessing all ornaments, holding a *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious vase) with her first left hand, a cluster of grain with the second, and a manuscript of the *Prajñāpāramitā* with the third.

From the complete transformation of the syllable *hrīḥ* meditated upon as emptiness, there arises a yellow lotus; upon that, from the syllable *āḥ*, a moon mandala; and again above that, from the complete transformation of the syllable *bhrūṃ*, a mountain of jewels; and above that, one should meditate on Vasudhārā from the seed-syllable *bhūṃ*.

Her body is yellow in color; she has one face and six arms and sits in a playful posture. She wears a crown of Tathāgatas. With her first right hand, she displays the mudrā of supreme generosity (*varada-mudrā*) while revealing treasures; with the second, she causes a rain of jewels to fall; and with the third, she pays homage to the Tathāgata Vajradhara Sāgaraghoṣa.
One should visualize [the deity] adorned with all ornaments, holding in the first left hand an excellent vase, in the second a cluster of rice ears, and in the third a volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

In the second enclosure, in the western direction, is the Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa. He is yellow and sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture. His left hand rests upon his lap, and his right hand is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*). To his right is Āryāvalokiteśvara, and to his left is Vajrapāṇi; both are red and green, with hands holding the boon-granting gesture and the vajra respectively. They stand in the royal ease posture (*rājalīlā*) with their left legs extended, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka. In the east is the goddess Īlādevī, yellow in color, presiding over all requisites.

To her left is Varuṇa, the presiding deity of taste, who is white; to her right is Bhadra, who is blue. In the southeast is Civikuṇḍalin, who is slightly red; in the southwest is Kelimālin, who is dark-maroon. In the northwest is Mukhendra, who is yellow; in the northeast is Carendra, who is fair-complexioned.

On the second panel, in the western direction, is the Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa, yellow in color, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with his left hand resting [on his lap] and his right hand performing the gesture of supreme generosity (varada-mudrā). To his right is the noble Avalokiteśvara.

To the left is Vajrapāṇi; these two are red and green respectively, with their right hands in the gesture of supreme generosity (*varada*) and holding vajras, while their left hands rest in the manner of royal play (*rāja-līlā*). They sit in the vajra-paryaṅka posture. To the east is the goddess Āryāṇī, yellow in color, who presides over all necessities. To her left is the Lord of Water (*Varuṇa*), white in color, who presides over the essence of flavors.

To his right is blue Jambhala; in the southeast is slightly reddish-orange Cipi Kuṇḍalī; in the southwest is greenish-blue Krimālimāraka; in the northwest is yellow Indriya; and in the northeast is whitish-yellow Caritrendriya.

In the third enclosure: in the southeast is the goddess Guptā, green in color, holding a *cāmara* in her hand; in the southwest is the goddess Suguptā, red, holding a parasol; in the northwest is the goddess Sarasvatī, yellow, holding a banner in her hand; in the northeast is the goddess Candrakāntā, white, holding a flag in her hand. In the east is Māṇibhadra, with the luster of saffron, holding a mongoose and a *bījapūraka* fruit in his hands; in the south is Pūrṇabhadra, blue, holding a pouch containing jewels and a *bījapūraka* fruit in his hands.

In the west is Dhanada, red in color, holding a *bhadraghaṭa* and a *bījapūraka* fruit in his hands. In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, yellow in color, holding a sprout of jewels and a *bījapūraka* fruit in his hands. All [the deities] sit in the sattva-paryaṅka posture. For those whose [attributes] have not been mentioned, they hold a *bījapūraka* fruit in their right hand and have their left hand resting on their lap. This is the sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities.

In the southeast (Agni) is the goddess Ljang gu, hidden within the three-fold woolen cloth; in the southwest (Nairṛti) is the red goddess Śin tu sbas pa, holding a parasol; in the northwest (Vāyu) is the yellow-gold goddess Sarasvatī, holding a banner in her hand; and in the northeast (Īśāna) is the white goddess Candrakāntamaṇi, bearing the mudrā of a banner.

In the east is Bhadra-pūrṇa, the color of saffron, holding a mongoose and a *vījapūraka* fruit as his mudrās. In the south is Ratnabhadra, possessing blue light, holding a jewel and a *vījapūraka* fruit as his mudrās. In the west is Vasudhārā, red in color, holding a fine vase and a *vījapūraka* fruit as her mudrās.

In the north is yellow Vaiśravaṇa, holding a jewel sprout and a *vījapūraka* fruit in his hands. All [deities] sit in the sattvaparyaṅka posture; as for those previously described, their right hands hold a *vījapūraka* fruit and their left hands rest upon their thighs. These are the sequence of the deities' visualization.

The root mantra of the Bhagavatī is: *oṃ vasudhāre svāhā*. The near-heart mantra is: *oṃ lakṣmībhūtalanivāsinīye svāhā*. For all [mantras], one should perform worship with a mantra that begins with the syllable *oṃ* and ends with *svāhā*, interwoven with their respective names. *Oṃ* at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end for all;
[the mantra] should be formed by interweaving the name of each deity with the *oṃ* at the start and *svāhā* at the end.
One should perform the offering with the mantras that proclaim each of their respective names.

Then, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family, with supreme faith, having spread out a cloth painting (*paṭa*) of the Vasudhārā image and worshipped it according to their means, should daily recite the *dhāraṇī* without interruption and with unbroken commitment.

Then, whichever son of noble family or daughter of noble family possesses supreme faith should fashion an image or a painted representation of Vasudhārā, perform offerings according to their means, and, remaining in meditative equipoise, recite the dhāraṇīs daily without interruption.
In due course, all forms of prosperity come to him.
By means of that sequence, one will achieve excellence in all respects.

Then, on the preceding day as well, having drawn a mandala with yellow pigment and having passed the night according to the prescribed rules, one should again, at dawn, bathe in fragrant water, become pure and clad in clean garments, and maintaining celibacy, spread out an image or a painting in an auspicious place; having made a small mandala with sandalwood paste, one should recite the Dhāraṇī together with its introduction three times without interruption.

Then, having prepared a mandala of yellow ochre from early morning, and having passed the night endowed with ascetic observances, one should again bathe with fragrant water at dawn, put on clean and stainless garments, and, having become pure in conduct, install a physical image or a painted scroll in an auspicious location.
Having prepared a sandalwood maṇḍala, one should recite the dhāraṇīs three times without interruption and without doubt.

Then, the house of that son of good family or daughter of good family becomes filled with a great man’s measure of wealth, with all kinds of riches, grain, silver, gold, and all necessary utensils; and it destroys all calamities.
In that case,

the household of that son of noble family or daughter of noble family will become filled with a stream of wealth to the extent of a great man’s measure— filled with all kinds of riches, grain, gold, silver, and all necessities— and all forms of harm will also cease to exist.

Alternatively, having drawn the mandala in that same manner, one should again at dawn—having bathed in fragrant water, being pure, clad in clean garments, abstaining from intoxicants and the like, eating no meat, avoiding salt, and observing celibacy—draw a square mandala with sandalwood paste for the sake of prosperity, either in one's own house, in another's house, or in an auspicious place such as a corner or a storehouse, in front of the Blessed Tathāgata, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the deity of the mantra.

Having performed a magnificent worship according to his means, the donor—well-composed, single-mindedly meditating upon that very Blessed Lady, and intent on the welfare and happiness [of others]—should, with supreme faith, recite this *dhāraṇī* together with its introduction for one day and night or for seven days and nights, without interruption and without speaking to others. [In the case of] the donor...?

Furthermore, having fashioned a circular maṇḍala within suchness, and having again performed an ablution with fragrant water as before, one should wear clean and stainless garments; being free from intoxicants and the like, and possessing pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) along with food that is blameless and not salty, one should proceed.

For the sake of enrichment, one should prepare a square sandalwood maṇḍala in one’s own home, another’s home, a virtuous place, or within a chamber or storeroom, and [therein worship] the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, and the noble Avalokiteśvara.

Having performed extensive offerings as they are available before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the deities of mantra, one should meditate upon that very Bhagavatī with a state of profound meditative equipoise.

With a one-pointed mind, possessing the intention for the benefit and happiness of the donor, and with faith and supreme freedom from doubt, one should recite this dhāraṇī continuously for one day and night, or for seven days and nights, without speaking with others.
In that same manner, the master, possessing the observance, should worship three times during the night and three times during the day with all offerings,
bali-oblations, and requisites.

In the same way, the patron (dānapati) should also undertake everything with disciplined observance (niyama). Furthermore, at the time of recitation, he should give gifts of gold and so forth to sentient beings according to his ability. Thereupon, it becomes accomplished through recitation.

Then, with a stream of wealth as vast as the earth and as great as the person of a Mahāpuruṣa, she completely fills the house of the donor with all kinds of riches, grain, silver, gold, and all necessary implements, and she destroys all calamities.

Merely by closing her eyes, Vasudhārā will completely fill the house of the donor with a stream of wealth befitting a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa)— with all kinds of riches, grain, gold, silver, and every necessary provision— and all forms of harm will also cease to exist.

Then, as before, one should dismiss the powder mandala and deposit all the powder into a treasury or storehouse; wherever the powder is deposited, everything there becomes inexhaustible. Furthermore, one should cause the banners, flags, and so forth to flow away into the waters of a river or similar body of water.

Then, as before, one should request the departure of the colored powder mandala; all the colored powder should be placed and kept within the storehouse of the house. Wherever the colored powder has been placed, there it shall remain inexhaustible. As for other items such as victory banners and flags, they should be cast into the waters of a river.
One should also satisfy the preceptors and others with blameless food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
and so forth.
This is the procedure for reciting the *Vasudhārā-dhāraṇī*.
This is the ritual for reciting the dhāraṇī of Vasudhārā.

"Noble son, this is that dhāraṇī called *Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijayā*, the great bearer of the staff of death, pure, and the destroyer of intoxication. It should be recited by anyone desiring long life according to the sequence to be described. On some spacious plot of ground, having smeared it with clay and cow dung, sprinkled it with fragrant water, and made it radiant with a canopy spread above, one should fashion a well-adorned eight-spoked wheel using white powders."

"Sons of noble family, this dhāraṇī called 'The Victory of the Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas' purifies those who undergo the great punishment of death and eliminates their misdeeds. Therefore, those who desire long life should recite it according to the ritual procedure for its exposition."

In a certain spacious location, having applied fresh clay and sprinkled it with fragrant water, one should spread a variegated canopy and decorate it by arranging an eight-spoked wheel with white colored powder.

In their midst, one should place the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa Prakṛtigarbha; and in sequence, in the spokes of the directions starting from the east, one should place Gaganasaṃnibhodayoṣṇīṣa, Kṣitigarbhodayoṣṇīṣa, Maṇigarbhodayoṣṇīṣa, Rajogarbhodayoṣṇīṣa, Amitagarbhodayoṣṇīṣa, Tejogarbhodayoṣṇīṣa, Dundubhisvarodayoṣṇīṣa, and Samīraṇodayoṣṇīṣa.

In its center is the Tathāgata Svabhāva-vipula-uṣṇīṣa; and in the spokes of the east and so forth, according to their sequence, there is the uṣṇīṣa arisen from space, the uṣṇīṣa arisen from Kṣitigarbha, and the uṣṇīṣa arisen from Ratnagarbha.

One should arrange the uṣṇīṣas arising from the essence of fire, the uṣṇīṣas arising from the immeasurable, the uṣṇīṣas arising from the essence of splendor, the uṣṇīṣas arising from the melody of the sound of drums, and the uṣṇīṣas arising from the essence of wind.

Outside of that, one should cause a well-proportioned sixteen-petaled lotus to be made. On each individual petal, one should sequentially place the sixteen Tathāgatas within sixteen moons: Uṣṇīṣa arising from internal emptiness; Uṣṇīṣa arising from external emptiness; Uṣṇīṣa arising from internal-and-external emptiness; Uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of emptiness; Uṣṇīṣa arising from ultimate emptiness; Uṣṇīṣa arising from conditioned emptiness; and Uṣṇīṣa arising from unconditioned emptiness.

The uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of non-dispersal; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of all phenomena; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of specific characteristics; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of non-apprehension; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of non-existence; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of self-nature; and the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

Outside of that, having fashioned a most beautiful sixteen-petaled lotus, one should place sixteen Tathāgatas upon each petal respectively, corresponding to the sixteen months: the Uṣṇīṣa arisen from internal emptiness, the Uṣṇīṣa arisen from external emptiness, and the Uṣṇīṣa arisen from internal-and-external emptiness.

The uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of emptiness; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of conditioned phenomena; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of that which transcends extremes; and the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.

The uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of non-affliction; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of all phenomena; the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of specific characteristics; and the uṣṇīṣa arising from the emptiness of the non-apprehendable.
The uṣṇīṣas arising from the emptiness of non-entities, the uṣṇīṣas arising from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the uṣṇīṣas arising from the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities.

Having constructed this maṇḍala of the Tathāgata’s seat and having arranged a scattering of flowers at the appropriate time, one should place upon it, atop the mechanical device (*yantrika*), a water vessel containing a caitya with Vairocana at its core. Inside, one should arrange a cluster of flowers at the appropriate time. Having constructed this maṇḍala of the Tathāgata’s seat, one should arrange a cluster of flowers at the appropriate time. Upon this, on top of the mechanical device, one should place a water vessel containing a caitya with Vairocana at its core.

Having inscribed the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) together with the mantra-water upon a golden leaf, one should place it there. One should fill [the vessel] with the water from the jar. Outside the lotus, four full jars should be placed in the four directions. Having adorned it with sprouts, umbrellas, and banners, furthermore: in the east, the goddess Uṣṇīṣavijayā who pacifies obstacles; in the south, the goddess Uṣṇīṣavijayā who pacifies death; in the west, the goddess Uṣṇīṣavijayā who pacifies the afflictions (*kleśa*).

In the north, one should place four vessels filled with fragrant water, mixed with perfumes, and adorned with hanging garlands, for the goddesses Uṣṇīṣavijayā—who pacifies ailments of the shoulders—and Āyurdātrī Vajramālā; in the southwest, Mahāmāyā; in the northwest, Kanakaprabhā; and in the northeast, Kāñcanamālikā Āyurdātrī. One should arrange them thus.

One should place the name of the person to be accomplished, interspersed with mantras, written clearly upon a golden tablet and set within; then, the vase should be filled with water. Four vases filled with water should be placed in the four directions outside the lotus. Having adorned it with foliage, umbrellas, and banners, [the ritual is completed].

Furthermore, in the east is the goddess Vijayā, who pacifies obstacles; in the south is the goddess Vijayā, who pacifies death; in the west is the goddess Vijayā, who pacifies afflictions; and in the north is the goddess Vijayā, who pacifies the diseases of the aggregates.

In the northeast, one should place Āyurdā Vajramālā; in the southeast, Mahāmāyā; in the northwest, Kanakaprabhā; and in the northeast, Āyurvardhanī Kanakamālā. Having filled four vessels with water mixed with fragrant scents, one should arrange them so that garlands of flowers hang down from each.

One should scatter colored powder within three lines. In the first row and so forth, one should have a thousand *caityas* made of rice-gruel and moist clay; if that is impossible, one should establish at least a hundred. Having performed worship with great honor in the four directions, and having taken *dūrvā* grass and *kunda* flowers, one should have the *dhāraṇī* recited by Dharma-preachers and install it after honoring each *caitya* at its summit.

One should worship by scattering unbroken rice, *dūrvā* grass, and a thousand jasmine flowers upon the summit of the central *caitya*. Having prepared a thousandfold array for each—namely, flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, offerings of food (*bali*), sacrificial cakes (*naivedya*), parasols, banners, and so forth—one should perform the worship with all these offerings. [In the case of the food, one should draw lines of dust.
(Note: A Dharma-preacher is commissioned to recite the *dhāraṇī*.)

Within the innermost of three concentric circles drawn with colored powders, one should fashion one thousand stupas made either of rice-gruel or clay; if these are not available, one hundred may be set out. One should perform extensive offerings for the sake of honoring [the deities] in the four directions. Holding durvā grass and kunda flowers, the reciter of the Dharma should recite this dhāraṇī.

One should perform worship upon the crowns of each stūpa and consecrate them. Having offered one thousand unbroken grains of rice, *dūrvā* grass, and *kunda* flowers onto the crowns of the central stūpa, one should perform worship.

One should perform a perfect offering by arranging each of all the offerings—such as flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, ritual cakes (bali), food, umbrellas, and banners—into a definite garland of one thousand each.

One should not remove the garland of lamps until its completion. One must always remain pure and composed in meditation. The Dharma-preachers, teachers, and Vajra-masters of the ritual must bathe with fragrant water and adorn themselves with white garments and ornaments. Remaining silent and facing the east, they should recite the text.

The Dharma-preacher, the Ācārya, [should ensure that] the row of lamps remains unextinguished for as long as it is complete; the incense sticks should remain unextinguished, and the offering substances should be maintained constantly. The Dharma-preacher, the Ācārya, and the Vajrakarmas, having bathed with fragrant water and adorned themselves with white garments and ornaments, should recite while remaining in meditative absorption and facing toward the east.
When this is done, one whose life span was seven days becomes one with a life span of seven years; one whose life span was seven years lives for seventy years; even untimely death is destroyed.
If one acts in this way, a lifespan of seven days will become a lifespan of seven years; a lifespan of seven years will become a lifespan of seventy years, and untimely death will no longer occur.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the recitation of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā.
Thus concludes the ritual for reciting the Uṣṇīṣavijayā.
